lesson.title: Learning from Data: The Fundamentals of Machine Learning
lesson.summary: Machine learning, the branch of AI in which computers learn patterns from data rather than explicit rules, developed through decades of foundational techniques before internet scale data and computing power unlocked its full potential.
lesson.body:
Machine learning is the branch of artificial intelligence in which computer systems improve their performance on a task by learning patterns from data, rather than following instructions that a programmer writes out explicitly for every situation. The term itself dates to 1959, when computer scientist Arthur Samuel used it to describe a checkers playing program that got better the more games it played, without a programmer updating its rules by hand.

Machine learning systems are generally grouped into a few broad categories. In supervised learning, a system learns from examples that are already labeled with the correct answer, such as thousands of emails marked spam or not spam, and it learns to predict the right label for new, unseen examples. In unsupervised learning, a system looks for patterns or groupings in data that has no labels at all, for example clustering customers with similar purchasing habits. In reinforcement learning, a system learns by trial and error, receiving rewards or penalties for actions it takes in an environment, similar in spirit to how Arthur Samuel's checkers program improved by playing games against itself.

Several foundational techniques developed over the following decades. Psychologist and computer scientist Frank Rosenblatt introduced the perceptron in 1957, an early type of artificial neural network loosely modeled on how biological neurons might process information, able to learn simple classification tasks. Researchers also developed other approaches during this period and in the following decades, including decision trees, which learn to make predictions through a series of branching yes or no questions, and support vector machines, a widely used technique developed and refined through the 1990s for classification problems. A particularly important advance came in 1986, when researchers David Rumelhart, Geoffrey Hinton, and Ronald Williams published a paper popularizing backpropagation, a mathematical method for efficiently training neural networks with more than one layer, which had previously been very difficult to do effectively.

For much of the twentieth century, machine learning's progress was limited less by the cleverness of its algorithms than by two practical constraints: the amount of data available to learn from and the computing power available to process it. Both constraints eased dramatically as the digital infrastructure built during the internet era matured, since the internet generated vast amounts of digital data, text, images, clicks, purchases, and more, while computing power kept increasing. This set the stage for the deep learning revolution, in which neural networks like Rosenblatt's perceptron, scaled up to many layers and trained on far larger datasets, achieved results that the field's earlier decades had not been able to reach.
